Instruments measure independent physical phenomena; observed weak correlations are random noise within chance levels

Observer or protocol bias (lab vs. observational) creates spurious correlations and method divergence
Resonator_obs measures a genuine ~4-day environmental cycle or structural resonance mode that other instruments do not couple to sensitively
Resonator_obs apparatus is miscalibrated, improperly damped, or operating at its own resonant frequency, producing instrumental ringing at ~4-day timescale

Resonator_lab and resonator_obs measure different physical quantities (e.g., resonant frequency vs. amplitude, or different modes) and require separate independent calibration baselines; cross-correlation reflects mode interference
Most cross-instrument and within-instrument correlations are noise within chance levels; resonator_obs 4-day signal is a statistical fluctuation (false positive)
Current sample size (n=8–24 post-baseline per instrument) is too small to distinguish weak real signals from noise; baseline must extend to day 20–30 before any hypothesis can be tested
Resonator_obs apparatus is miscalibrated, improperly damped, or ringing at its own resonant frequency, producing instrumental artifact at ~4-day timescale

Resonator_obs and resonator_lab measure different physical quantities (e.g., resonant frequency vs. amplitude, or orthogonal modes) and require independent calibration; apparent anti-correlation reflects mode interference or phase lag
Resonator_obs measures a genuine ~4-day environmental cycle or structural resonance (thermal, seismic, or building mode) that other instruments do not couple to sensitively
Most observed correlations and level shifts are statistical noise within chance levels; resonator_obs 4-day signal is a false positive from small-n multiple comparisons

Post-baseline sample size (n=8–24 per instrument, n=14–68 for resonator_obs) is too small to distinguish weak real signals from noise; baseline must extend to day 20–30 before any hypothesis can be tested rigorously
Resonator_obs apparatus underwent a state change (damping, tuning, or electronics) around day 26, causing persistent or episodic elevation in measured cycles/beat

Resonator_obs and resonator_lab measure mechanically or electrically orthogonal observables (e.g., frequency vs. amplitude, or two cavity modes); day-26 excursion reflects mode-dependent response to an environmental perturbation
Day-26 excursion is noise within resonator_obs's expected measurement variance; no state change or environmental event is implied
Resonator_obs apparatus requires independent recalibration; baseline established on days 1–10 does not account for drift or hysteresis and is not valid for post-day-10 data
Genuine environmental or structural event (thermal pulse, seismic noise, or transient building resonance) on day 26 coupled differentially to resonator_obs but not to lab instruments or resonator_lab

Systematic baseline artifact: day-1–10 baseline established under transient conditions (thermal equilibration, apparatus cold-start, observer unfamiliarity) not representative of steady-state apparatus behavior post-day-10.

Each instrument measures a distinct physical quantity (not all the same underlying 'time') and cross-correlations are weak because they respond to different environmental drivers or have independent instrumental noise.

Post-baseline drift is within expected measurement noise; the z-values (0.90–1.48) are marginally significant and the 'drift' is an optical illusion from small sample size (post-baseline n=54–318) and p-hacking of baseline definition.

Observer or procedural bias introduced post-day-10: recording technique changed, observer rotated, or calibration standard was unknowingly altered, causing a systematic shift in reported readings across all instruments.

Common environmental signal (daily or multi-day thermal cycle, barometric drift, or building resonance from external activity) couples to all instruments with similar lag and phase, but cross-correlations are low because signal-to-noise ratio is poor and lags vary between instrument pairs.

Systematic baseline artifact: day-1–10 baseline corrupted by cold-start transients (thermal cycling, mechanical settling, calibration hysteresis, observer learning), yielding artificially low baseline mean; post-day-10 readings represent true steady-state apparatus equilibrium.

Each instrument measures a distinct physical observable (not all the same underlying quantity), with independent instrumental noise and environmental coupling; weak cross-correlations reflect orthogonal measurement targets rather than measurement error or systematic error.

Post-baseline drift is within expected measurement noise (Type I error); z-values of 0.90–1.48 correspond to 7–18% tail probabilities for single instruments, and with four instruments and multiple analyses (p-hacking via baseline definition or lag-searching), one or two false positives are expected.

Procedural or observer change introduced post-day-10 (new observer, calibration artifact removed, measurement protocol drift) caused systematic upward shift in reported readings across all instruments, explaining coordinated drift without requiring apparatus settling.

Common external environmental signal (thermal cycle, barometric drift, building vibration) couples to all instruments with similar amplitude but variable lag and phase due to different mechanical/thermal time constants, explaining coordinated drift; weak cross-correlations reflect poor signal-to-noise ratio and lag variability between pairs.
